title: Innovation and Emerging Technology
description: Introducing AI, automation, platforms, or **emerging technology** with disciplined experimentation, adoption, risk management, and measurable impact.

competency.name: Innovation and Emerging Technology
competency.definition: Evaluates and adopts new technology through evidence, risk controls, behavior change, and **measurable outcomes**.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior leaders must separate useful innovation from hype while creating conditions for **responsible adoption**.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you introduced a new technology that changed how your organization worked.
variants: Describe how you evaluated whether AI, automation, or a new platform capability was worth adopting.
Tell me about a time a technology experiment did not justify broader rollout.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate test **emerging technology** with discipline?
Do they manage security, quality, adoption, and change management?
Can they measure impact beyond excitement or license usage?

scenario.signatureExample: A senior leader introduces AI-assisted development tools with security rules, cycle-time measurement, code-review quality checks, and team training.
context: Engineers are experimenting individually with AI tools.
Security and legal teams are concerned about data exposure.
Executives want productivity gains but lack evidence.
constraints: The organization needs guardrails before broad adoption.
Impact must be measured without vanity metrics.
Teams need training and workflow changes, not just licenses.

storyAnatomy.situation: The organization had fragmented AI-tool usage with enthusiasm, risk concerns, and unclear productivity impact.
storyAnatomy.task: Evaluate and scale AI-assisted development responsibly if evidence justified it.
action: Defined acceptable-use, security, and code-review policies.
Ran a pilot with control groups and measured cycle time, review quality, defects, and developer experience.
Trained teams on effective use cases and prohibited uses.
Adjusted rollout based on evidence rather than initial enthusiasm.
result: The organization adopted the tools where impact was measurable.
Security and quality concerns were addressed through guardrails.
Teams learned where AI helped and where human review remained critical.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The lesson was that innovation adoption is an operating change, not a procurement event.

exampleStories.title: AI-Assisted Development Adoption
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you introduced a new technology that changed how your organization worked.
exampleStories.situation: Engineers were already experimenting with AI coding tools, executives wanted productivity gains, and Security was concerned about code and data exposure.
strongAnswerSketch: Define the adoption hypothesis and acceptable-use policy.
Run a pilot measuring cycle time, review quality, defects, and developer experience.
Train teams on effective and prohibited use cases.
Scale adoption only where evidence and guardrails support it.
whyItWorks: Manages quality and security risks during adoption.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I bought AI coding licenses, encouraged teams to experiment, and tracked adoption to see whether people found value.

exampleStories.title: Internal Platform Trial
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time a technology experiment did not justify broader rollout.
exampleStories.situation: A platform team piloted a new deployment abstraction that improved one team experience but made debugging harder for services with unusual runtime needs.
strongAnswerSketch: Define success criteria before the pilot: lead time, failure recovery, support load, and developer satisfaction.
Measure both happy-path adoption and operational friction.
Decide not to roll out broadly until debugging and escape-hatch problems are solved.
Document adoption criteria for the next platform experiment.
whyItWorks: Shows willingness to stop an exciting technology.
Measures operational consequences, not only developer enthusiasm.
exampleStories.weakVersion: The pilot feedback was mixed, so we delayed rollout and gave the platform team more time to improve it.
followUpAngles: Who was disappointed by the decision?
What did the next pilot do differently?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows **experimentation discipline**, adoption strategy, risk management, and measurable impact.
moves: Includes risk, security, and quality controls.
Measures behavior and outcomes, not only adoption.
Invests in training and workflow integration.
Scales, changes, or stops based on evidence.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate treats innovation as buying tools or following trends without disciplined evaluation or adoption design.
redFlags: Uses hype language without a testable hypothesis.
Cannot name conditions under which they would stop rollout.

followUps.question: What risks did you control before adoption?
How did you measure impact beyond usage?
What changed in how teams actually worked?

signals.name: Experimentation Discipline
signals.strong: Defines hypotheses, metrics, risks, and rollout criteria.
signals.weak: Runs broad adoption based on enthusiasm.

signals.name: Risk-Aware Adoption
signals.strong: Integrates security, quality, and responsible-use guardrails.
signals.weak: Treats risk as a later compliance concern.

rubric.expected: Pilots technology within a team with clear metrics and guardrails.
Scales adoption across teams through training, workflow changes, and impact measurement.
Creates an organizational adoption model for **emerging technology** with risk controls and portfolio impact.
Sets company-level technology adoption strategy balancing strategic leverage, risk, and operating change.

prompts.label: What new technology or capability was being considered?
What adoption or evaluation decision did you own?
How did you test, control risk, train, and measure?
What evidence justified scaling, changing, or stopping?
What did you learn about technology adoption?
What adoption framework or guardrail remained?

relatedScenarios: Evaluating AI support tools for customer operations.
Stopping a technology rollout after pilot evidence disappoints.
